title: Nielsen Norman Group, Inverted Pyramid: Writing for Comprehension
text:
## Definition and Origin
The inverted pyramid is a journalistic writing structure in which the most important information, or what might even be considered the conclusion, is presented first. The name comes from picturing broad, essential facts at the top of the pyramid, then narrowing to smaller supporting details below, like a triangle balanced on its point. It was developed by journalists so that a story communicated its core even if a reader stopped after the first sentence or if an editor cut the piece from the bottom.

## Why It Works for Web Content
The structure suits web reading because users do not read carefully online and have limited patience for unengaging content. The inverted pyramid addresses these patterns by improving comprehension (readers quickly form a mental model before encountering supporting details), decreasing interaction cost (main points are understood without extensive reading), encouraging scrolling (an engaging opening draws readers into the details below), supporting skimmers (readers can stop reading at any point on the page and still come away with the main point), and enabling easy editing (content can be trimmed at nearly any point without losing essential information).

## Application Strategy
A five step approach: first, identify the single key fact readers should retain, expressible in one sentence or paragraph. Second, rank secondary information by how broadly the audience cares about it. Third, write concisely using straightforward language and short paragraphs. Fourth, frontload every element: headlines, opening sentences, and the initial words of each should carry the information that indicates what follows. Fifth, consider adding a summary section or highlighted key points so the conclusion is unmissable. The core discipline is to lead with the conclusion, not build up to it.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Information Scent: How Users Decide Where to Go Next
text:
## Definition and Theory
Information scent is the user's imperfect estimate of the value that a source will deliver, derived from a representation of that source (for example a link label and its surrounding context). It comes from information foraging theory, developed by Pirolli and Card, which explains how people navigate based on their assessment of (1) how relevant a page seems and (2) how much time it will take to find the answer. The analogy is to animal foraging: just as scent guides animals toward food, information cues guide users toward relevant pages.

## Four Core Components
Information scent involves the actual source (the page itself), the remote representation (the link label and its context), the true value (unknown until the content is consumed), and the estimated value (what the user judges before clicking).

## Factors Affecting Information Scent
Link labels should be a succinct yet accurate description of what the page is about. Clear, self explanatory labels strongly affect click decisions, while jargon and obscure terminology reduce scent regardless of accuracy. Accompanying content such as summary text and images should reinforce the link label with relevant detail; generic or loosely related imagery diminishes scent, and category images work best when they show a prototypical example rather than an unusual one. Contextual cues from surrounding page content also shape how a link is perceived, but relying only on context is risky, especially on mobile where less is visible at once. A user's prior knowledge raises scent through brand familiarity and trust, domain expertise, and previous positive experiences.

## Social Foraging and Clickbait Warning
Reviews and recommendations from other users augment information scent. Misleading headlines that misrepresent content erode trust permanently. Strong brands have slightly more tolerance for the occasional miss, but consistency between what a link promises and what the page delivers remains essential. The practical lesson for writers: make link text, headings, and opening lines carry a strong, honest signal of what the reader will get.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, How Chunking Helps Content Processing
text:
## Definition and Core Concept
Chunking originates in cognitive psychology and refers to organizing information into meaningful units. A chunk is an organizational unit in memory; in UX design, chunking means breaking up content into small, distinct units of information. Presenting content in chunks makes scanning easier and can improve a user's ability to comprehend and remember it.

## Cognitive Psychology Foundation
George Miller's 1956 research found people can retain about 7 chunks of information in short term memory. Chunk size is flexible: people could remember either 7 individual letters, or 28 letters if they were grouped into 7 four letter words. A key misconception is that the magical number seven should limit design choices such as the number of navigation items. Miller's actual insight is the opposite: if you want users to retain more, pack information into meaningful chunks.

## Text Chunking Methods
Effective techniques include short paragraphs separated by white space, text lines of roughly 50 to 75 characters, clear visual hierarchies that group related items, and distinct groupings within strings such as phone numbers, passwords, and credit cards. Use the most conventional format for each data type to minimize user slips; for example a credit card typically displays as 4111 1111 1111 1111 rather than as an unpunctuated run of digits.

## Supporting Scannability and Limitations
Beyond formatting, support scanning with headings that have clear contrast, highlighted keywords, bulleted or numbered lists, and summary paragraphs for longer sections. Apply the Law of Proximity by keeping related elements close together using background color, rules, and white space; this extends to chunking videos into navigable chapters and grouping related tools in a toolbar. The article cautions that short term memory capacity varies significantly among individuals and depends on context, existing expertise, and environment, not just a theoretical limit.

title: Mailchimp Content Style Guide, Voice and Tone
text:
## Voice vs. Tone Distinction
Mailchimp separates voice from tone with a simple analogy: voice stays consistent, while tone shifts with context. Just as a person speaks differently to a close friend than to a boss, the writing adjusts its tone to the reader's emotional state while keeping one underlying voice.

## Mailchimp's Voice Characteristics
The brand writes as an experienced, plainspoken business partner. Its voice principles include plainspoken clarity (stripping away hyperbolic language, upsells, and over promises so clarity comes first, avoiding emotional manipulation and flowery language), genuine relatability (connecting with small businesses through familiar, warm, accessible language rooted in shared experience), the expert translator role (demystifying complex terminology and making difficult concepts accessible), and dry humor (straight faced, subtle, and a touch eccentric; weird but not inappropriate, smart but not snobbish; subtle wit over overt comedy).

## Tone Application
Writers should read the reader's emotional state and adjust to it. The tone is usually informal, but clarity always takes priority over entertainment. Humor works when it is natural and appropriate; a forced joke underperforms silence.

## Writing Principles
Three style elements guide execution: use active voice rather than passive constructions, use plain English by eliminating slang and jargon, and use positive framing by preferring affirmative statements over negative ones. The larger lesson for content writers is that a documented voice plus context aware tone is what makes a brand sound like one coherent person across every screen.

title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, Writing for Web Accessibility
text:
## Provide Informative, Unique Page Titles
Provide a short title that describes the page content and distinguishes it from other pages. Put the most relevant information first, for example the page name before the organization name. For a multi step process, include the current step. Example: Buy Your Bear (Step 1 of 3), Space Teddy Inc.

## Use Headings to Convey Meaning and Structure
Use short headings to group related paragraphs and clearly describe the sections. Good headings provide an outline of the content and are essential for screen reader users to navigate. They must be semantically tagged, not merely styled to look different, so assistive technology recognizes them as structure.

## Make Link Text Meaningful
Write link text so that it describes the content of the link target. Avoid vague phrases like click here or read more. Include relevant details such as document type and file size. Example: instead of click here, use Read more about device independence.

## Write Meaningful Text Alternatives for Images
For every image, write alternative text that provides the information or function of the image. Decorative images do not need alt text. Example: use Plug cable into the bottom edge of the phone rather than a generic Charging phone.

## Create Transcripts and Captions for Multimedia
Provide transcripts for audio only content and captions for audio visual content. Include spoken information and sounds that are important for understanding, plus descriptions of significant visual content.

## Provide Clear Instructions and Keep Content Concise
Ensure that instructions, guidance, and error messages are clear, easy to understand, and avoid unnecessarily technical language. Write in short, clear sentences and paragraphs; avoid unnecessarily complex words and phrases; expand acronyms on first use, for example Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG); consider providing a glossary for unfamiliar terms; and use lists, images, illustrations, and symbols to help clarify meaning. Accessible writing overlaps almost entirely with good plain writing.

title: Google Search Central, Spam Policies (Keyword Stuffing and Related)
text:
## Keyword Stuffing (Anti-Pattern)
Keyword stuffing refers to the practice of filling a web page with keywords or numbers in an attempt to manipulate rankings in Google Search results. Examples include lists of phone numbers without substantial added value, blocks of text that list the cities and regions a page is trying to rank for, and unnaturally repeating the same words or phrases, such as overusing app store credit multiple times in one paragraph. Google flags content that sounds unnatural and lacks context. The lesson for writers: write for the reader in natural language, never pad a page with repeated terms.

## Scaled Content Abuse and Thin Content (Anti-Patterns)
Scaled content abuse means generating many pages without adding value for users, whether by automation, AI tools, or manual effort. It includes scraping and reformatting feeds, stitching together content from multiple sources without adding original value, and creating pages with little coherence that merely contain search keywords. Thin content provides little original value, particularly in affiliate contexts where product descriptions are copied straight from merchants without meaningful additions or original review.

## Doorway Pages, Hidden Text, and Cloaking (Anti-Patterns)
Doorway abuse funnels users through intermediate pages or near duplicate URLs that target specific queries rather than sending them straight to useful destinations. Hidden text and links place content on a page solely to manipulate search engines and not to be easily viewable by human visitors, using tricks like white text on a white background, text hidden behind an image, CSS to push text off screen, or font size and opacity set to zero. Cloaking presents different content to users and to search engines with the intent to manipulate rankings and mislead people. All of these substitute algorithm gaming for genuine, honest content, which is exactly what a top content writer avoids.

title: Google Search Central, Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content
text:
## Core Philosophy
Google's ranking systems prioritize helpful, reliable information that is created to benefit people, and not content that is created to manipulate search engine rankings. The recommended test is to write people first content, not search engine first content.

## Self-Assessment: Content and Quality
Ask: Does the content provide original information, reporting, research, or analysis? Does it offer a substantial, complete description of the topic? Does it provide insightful analysis beyond the obvious? If it draws on other sources, does it add substantial value rather than simply copying? Does the main heading provide a descriptive, helpful summary without exaggeration? Is this something you would bookmark, share, or recommend? Would it appear in a printed magazine, encyclopedia, or book? Does it provide substantial value compared to other results? Is it well produced, or does it look sloppy or hastily made?

## People-First Content: Five Questions
Answering yes indicates people first content. Do you have an existing or intended audience who would find this useful if they came to you directly? Does the content demonstrate first hand expertise and depth of knowledge? Does your site have a primary purpose or focus? After reading, will someone feel they learned enough to help achieve their goal? Will readers feel they had a satisfying experience?

## Search-Engine-First Warning Signs (Anti-Pattern)
Avoid content made mainly to attract search visits, signaled by producing lots of content on many topics hoping some ranks, using automation to mass produce, mainly summarizing others without adding value, writing about trending topics you have no real audience for, leaving readers needing to search again for better information, writing to a target word count because you heard the algorithm prefers it, entering a niche with no genuine expertise, promising to answer a question that has no answer, and changing dates to look fresh without substantial updates.

## Who, How, and Why, plus E-E-A-T
Make the Who clear through bylines and author background. Explain the How of production, especially any automation or AI, and disclose when automation substantially generated content. The Why should be to help people, not to game rankings, and this is the most important consideration. E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness; Trust is the most important member, and systems weight E-E-A-T more heavily for Your Money or Your Life topics affecting health, finances, safety, or societal welfare.

title: Ann Handley, 13 Writing Rules (Everybody Writes)
text:
## Ann Handley's 13 Writing Rules
These rules from Everybody Writes are the working philosophy of one of the most recognized voices in content marketing.

1. There is no one way to write, just as there is no one way to parent a child or roast a turkey.
2. Our words are our emissaries; they tell the world who we are.
3. Good writing isn't just any tool. It's the power tool you should be able to wield expertly, just as every respectable building contractor can use the skilsaw he keeps in his truck.
4. The key to being a better writer is to be a more productive one. More simply: the key to being a better writer is to write.
5. Writing well is part habit, part knowledge of some fundamental rules, and part giving a damn.
6. No one will ever complain that you've made things too simple to understand.
7. Assume the reader knows nothing, but don't assume the reader is stupid.
8. Buzzwords and jargon are the chemical additives of writing.
9. The Ugly First Draft isn't a pass you give yourself to produce substandard work, but it is a necessary part of the process of creating above standard work.
10. The people you think of as good writers are often terrible writers on their first drafts. But here's their secret: they are excellent editors of their own work.
11. Editing is not just about fixing the grammar, it's about fixing the clarity for your reader.
12. You can't rush art is folly. You do have to rush your art. Otherwise that art sits on its butt on the couch watching Netflix.
13. Deadlines are the WD-40 of writing.

## Why This Matters
Rules 9, 10, and 11 encode the single most important habit in professional writing: separate drafting from editing. Write badly and fast first (the Ugly First Draft), then edit ruthlessly for clarity. Rules 6, 7, and 8 are the anti-jargon, pro-simplicity stance that defines strong web writing.

title: Ann Handley, A Writing GPS (Step-by-Step Guide to Creating Content)
text:
## The Writing GPS
Ann Handley's Writing GPS is a step by step framework from her book Everybody Writes that guides a writer from discombobulated thoughts to a coherent, cogent piece of writing that others can grok and maybe love. It is meant for longer text such as blog posts, e-books, white papers, and site content. The point of a GPS is to give you a sense of the path you are taking so the journey is less anxious.

## Key Moves in the Process
The Ugly First Draft (TUFD): write without self censorship first, because you are going to change it anyway; just get something down. The So What question: interrogate every draft by asking whether the reader will care and why this matters to them. Walking away: step back from the draft temporarily to create distance for objective review and revision. Write to one person rather than to a generic audience, which personalizes the voice and strengthens connection. Handley frames writing as navigating a very dark, very long tunnel (a reference to Andre Dubus), arguing that structure is what transforms raw ideas into communication others can understand.

## Practical Takeaway
The discipline is process over inspiration: separate generating from refining, always test relevance with So What, and address a single real reader instead of a faceless crowd.

title: Kristina Halvorson, The Discipline of Content Strategy (A List Apart)
text:
## Core Definition
Kristina Halvorson defines content strategy as plans for the creation, publication, and governance of useful, usable content. A strategist must define not just what content to publish, but why, or the effort becomes merely a glorified production line for content nobody really needs or wants.

## Six Interrelated Practices
Rather than treating content strategy as one thing, Halvorson delineates six practices. Editorial strategy establishes governance guidelines covering voice, tone, values, legal considerations, and content lifecycles. Web writing means crafting content specifically for online audiences, which requires understanding of UX, information architecture, and metadata. Metadata strategy structures data about data to enable meaningful content organization and reuse across channels. Search engine optimization organizes page content and metadata to increase relevance to search keywords. Content management strategy selects the technologies for capturing, storing, and delivering content. Content channel distribution strategy determines how and where audiences access content.

## Central Arguments
Halvorson contends the web industry has obsessed over UX and design while neglecting content itself, which is why web content is, for the most part, crap. She advocates recognizing content's strategic value and allocating appropriate time, budget, and expertise to planning and governance rather than treating content as an afterthought. The through line for a content writer: substance (what to say) and structure (how it is organized and tagged) both need a plan, and someone must own the ongoing governance.

title: CoSchedule, How to Write Headlines (Word Balance and Emotional Value)
text:
## The Four Word Categories
CoSchedule's headline research recommends balancing words from four categories. Common words (20 to 30 percent) are ones you use all the time and provide the structural foundation for readability. Uncommon words (10 to 20 percent) are distinctive terms that grab your readers' attention and add substance. Emotional words (10 to 15 percent) evoke feeling and entice the audience to click through, increasing shareability. Power words (at least 1) are phrases well known for inciting action, rarely used terms that inspire engagement without needing context.

## Length Recommendations
Headlines around 55 characters receive the highest click through rates, though Google now displays up to 70 characters in search results. For email subject lines, place keywords in the first 20 characters before the text truncates. Word count of 6 to 7 words typically performs best, with 10 words as the practical maximum. Critically, the first three and last three words receive most of the reader's attention, so load meaning there.

## Emotional Value and Target Score
Strongly positive sentiment outperforms neutral or negative tones; headlines conveying very strong emotions generate the best results, with positive sentiment producing more shares. CoSchedule advises aiming for a headline analyzer score of 70 or above on a 0 to 100 scale.

## Takeaway
A good headline is engineered, not guessed: mix readable, attention grabbing, emotional, and action words, put the strongest words first and last, and remember that the headline is the highest leverage sentence you write because most people decide from it alone whether to read on. This tactical layer sits on top of the older classic rule that on average five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy.

title: Jakob Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (Nielsen Norman Group)
text:
## Core Finding
Users do not read web pages word by word. Instead they scan the page, picking out individual words and sentences. This is the seminal study behind web writing practice.

## Key Statistic
Research found that 79 percent of test users always scanned any new page they came across; only 16 percent read word by word.

## Web Writing Recommendations
To accommodate scanning, Nielsen recommends highlighted keywords (hyperlinks, typeface variations, and color count as highlighting), meaningful subheadings rather than clever ones, bulleted lists, one idea per paragraph (users skip over additional ideas if they are not caught by the first few words), the inverted pyramid style starting with the conclusion, and half the word count of conventional writing (or less).

## Against Marketese
Users rejected marketese, the promotional writing style full of boastful subjective claims such as hottest ever. Promotional language imposes a cognitive burden because readers have to spend resources filtering out the hyperbole to get at the facts.

## Measurable Impact
A site version that combined concise, scannable, and objective writing measured 124 percent better in usability than the promotional control version. The three levers, concise (about half the words), scannable (structured for the eye), and objective (plain not promotional), each improved usability and combined for the largest gain.

title: Purdue OWL, AP Style Overview
text:
## What AP Style Is
Associated Press style provides guidelines for news writing. Many newspapers, magazines, and public relations offices across the United States use AP style. Its guiding principles are consistency, clarity, accuracy, and brevity, and it aims to avoid stereotypes and unintentionally offensive language.

## Numbers and Figures
Never start a sentence with a figure, except for a year. Spell out numbers below 10 and use figures for 10 and above. For money use numerals, and spell out cents, million, and billion for amounts of one million dollars and above.

## Dates and Times
Use figures for dates and years and omit the ordinal suffixes st, nd, rd, th. Abbreviate only Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec. when used with a specific date. Use an apostrophe before a decade when numerals are omitted, as in the '90s. For times use figures with a colon separating hours and minutes, spell out noon and midnight, and drop the :00, as in 1 p.m. and 3:30 a.m.

## Titles, Punctuation, Abbreviations
Capitalize formal titles directly before a name and lowercase titles that follow a name or are set off by commas. Use a single space after a period. Do not use a comma before the conjunction in a simple series (AP omits the Oxford comma). Commas and periods go within quotation marks. Use required courtesy or professional titles such as Dr. and Sen. on first reference, and avoid alphabet soup by minimizing unnecessary acronyms. The point for content writers: a house style guide is what keeps a brand's numbers, dates, and terms consistent across every writer and every page.

title: Readable, Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level
text:
## The Two Formulas
The Flesch Reading Ease scores text on a scale where the higher the score, the easier the text is to read. The Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level converts readability into a US school grade, so a score of 8 means the reader needs a grade 8 reading level or above to understand it. Both formulas analyze two factors: sentence length (average words per sentence) and word length (average syllables per word). Shorter sentences and shorter words produce easier, higher scoring text.

## Grade Level Bands
Approximate Flesch-Kincaid bands: 0 to 3 basic, kindergarten to early elementary, ages 5 to 8; 3 to 6 basic elementary, ages 8 to 11; 6 to 9 average middle school, ages 11 to 14; 9 to 12 average high school, ages 14 to 17; 12 to 15 advanced college, ages 17 to 20; 15 to 18 advanced post graduate, ages 20 and up.

## Recommended Target
Text intended for the general public should aim for a grade level of around 8, schooling age 13 to 14. Writing above that level shrinks the audience who can comfortably read it, which is why plain writing and readability testing are core content skills, not dumbing down. The practical workflow: draft, then run a readability check, then cut sentence length and swap long words for short ones until the score matches the audience.

title: William Zinsser, On Simplicity and Clutter (On Writing Well, excerpted)
text:
## The Secret of Good Writing (Anti-Clutter)
William Zinsser, in On Writing Well, states that the secret of good writing is to strip every sentence to its cleanest components. Every word that serves no function, every long word that could be a short word, every adverb that carries the same meaning that is already in the verb, every passive construction that leaves the reader unsure of who is doing what: these are the thousand and one adulterants that weaken the strength of a sentence.

## Clear Thinking, Clear Writing
Clear thinking becomes clear writing; one cannot exist without the other. The clear writer is someone clearheaded enough to see this stuff for what it is: fuzz.

## Writing Is Hard Work
Writing is hard work. A clear sentence is no accident. Very few sentences come out right the first time, or even the third time.

## The Anti-Pattern
The failure mode Zinsser names is clutter: unnecessary words, circular constructions, pompous frills, and meaningless jargon that bury the meaning. The remedy is ruthless subtraction. For a content writer this is the single highest leverage editing habit: after the ugly first draft, cut every word, phrase, and passive construction that does not earn its place. Simplicity is not simplistic; it is the result of hard editing and clear thinking.

title: Knowadays, The Inverted Pyramid in Journalism (Burying the Lede)
text:
## Definition
The inverted pyramid is a structural approach in journalism and business writing that prioritizes information by importance, placing critical details at the beginning and less essential background toward the end.

## The Lead (or Lede)
The opening line or paragraph must answer the who, what, why, where, when, and how of the subject matter in no more than one or two sentences. This ensures readers immediately grasp the main point, which especially benefits those who skim.

## Burying the Lede (Anti-Pattern)
Burying the lede is an editorial mistake that occurs when key facts are placed deeper within the piece rather than prominently featured at the start. Editors should verify that essential information appears upfront, not hidden later in the article. It is one of the most common web writing failures: readers who scan will never reach a point that is buried below the fold.

## The Three-Tier Structure
The Lead contains all the necessary information for understanding the core story. The Body provides supporting details, evidence, quotes, and expanded context without introducing new essential facts. The Tail includes optional background information and helpful but non critical insights.

## Why This Serves Scanners
Because many readers skim online content, the inverted pyramid enables quick comprehension of the main idea without requiring full engagement, which particularly helps mobile readers who avoid scrolling through long paragraphs. Lead with the answer, then justify it, never build up to the point.

title: Content Marketing Institute, Editorial Calendar Fundamentals
text:
## What It Is and Why It Matters
An editorial calendar is the tool most critical for effectively managing a content marketing program. It tracks content creation tasks and the status of each piece through production stages, while also streamlining collaboration, monitoring performance, and revealing repurposing opportunities.

## Essential Elements to Track
Each calendar entry should document publication timing (date and publishing schedule), content identification (headline and topic or category), ownership (author and workflow manager or approver), format and distribution (content type and channels), performance data (target keywords, CTAs, and KPIs), production status (current workflow stage and due dates), and visual requirements (cover images, videos, or other assets).

## Setup Approaches
Teams can choose from spreadsheet tools such as Google Sheets or Excel, project management platforms such as Asana, Trello, or Airtable, or dedicated editorial workflow software. Spreadsheets offer simplicity but limited integration; specialized tools provide advanced features but require more investment. The Content Marketing Institute itself uses a Google Sheet template that tracks headline, author, topic, and workflow status for daily blog publication.

## Recommended Practices
Beyond basic scheduling, a calendar should capture story ideas, track contributor details, support cross departmental collaboration, and maintain performance analytics for reporting. The governing lesson: assign owners, not just due dates, because a due date with no owner is a wish. A calendar turns a content strategy into a repeatable operating cadence.

title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, Top 10 Tips for Style and Voice
text:
## Use Bigger Ideas, Fewer Words
Modern style hinges on crisp minimalism; shorter is always better. Example: replace If you're ready to purchase Office 365 for your organization, contact your Microsoft account representative with Ready to buy? Contact us.

## Write Like You Speak
Read your text aloud. Avoid jargon and overly complex or technical language. It should sound like a friendly conversation. Replace Invalid ID with You need an ID that looks like this: someone@example.com.

## Project Friendliness
Use contractions like it's, you'll, you're, we're, and let's, so the writing sounds warm and human rather than stiff.

## Get to the Point Fast
Lead with what's most important. Front-load keywords for scanning. Make customer choices and next steps obvious. This is the front-loading principle: the first words of a heading, sentence, or link should carry the meaning.

## Be Brief
Give readers just enough information to make decisions confidently, and prune every excess word.

## When in Doubt, Don't Capitalize
Default to sentence style capitalization: capitalize only the first word of a heading or phrase plus any proper nouns. Do not use title style capitalization.

## Use End Punctuation in the Right Places
Do not use a period or a colon at the end of titles, headings, subheadings, and UI titles.

## Remember the Last Comma
In a list of three or more items, include a comma before the conjunction (the Oxford or serial comma). Replace Android, iOS and Windows with Android, iOS, and Windows. Note that this is the opposite of AP style, which omits the serial comma; the lesson is that a house style must pick one rule and apply it everywhere.

## Don't Be Spacey
Use only one space after periods, question marks, and colons, and no spaces around em dashes.

## Revise Weak Writing
Most of the time, start each statement with a verb. Edit out you can when it is not necessary, and avoid weak phrasing like there is, there are, and there were. Replace You can access Office apps across your devices, and you get online file storage and sharing with Store files online, access them from all your devices, and share them with coworkers.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, How People Read Online (Scanning Patterns)
text:
## The Core Behavior
People rarely read online; they are far more likely to scan than to read word for word. This has remained constant for over 23 years of eyetracking research, regardless of technology changes.

## Scanning Patterns
The F-pattern: users scan the upper portion of the page horizontally, then move down the left side, tracing an F shaped path (common on text heavy pages with little formatting). The layer-cake pattern: the eye moves across headings and subheadings in horizontal bands, skipping the paragraphs between them (this is the pattern good formatting produces). The spotted pattern: readers jump to specific elements such as links, numbers, or bolded words rather than following a line. The commitment pattern: sustained attention to a section the reader is highly motivated by. The bypassing pattern: readers deliberately skip the first words of lines when several lines start with the same word. The zigzag and, on modern layouts, the lawn-mower and pinball patterns describe non linear movement across grids and search results.

## Supporting Effective Scanning
Because scanning dominates, write for it: use clear, noticeable headings and subheadings, front-load information by putting the important content up front, use formatting such as bulleted lists and bold text to emphasize key points, and use plain language. The layer-cake finding is the actionable one for writers: strong, meaningful subheadings let a scanning reader assemble the gist from the headings alone, so every subheading must carry real information.

title: Mailchimp Content Style Guide, Grammar and Mechanics
text:
## Writing for All Readers
Write for all readers. Some people will read every word you write; others will just skim. Group related ideas together, use descriptive headers and subheaders, and lead with the main point so skimmers still get it.

## Active Voice
Use active voice. In active voice, the subject of the sentence does the action. Avoid passive voice, where the subject receives the action and constructions rely on was and by. The occasional exception is when you deliberately want to emphasize the action over the actor.

## Positive Language
Use positive language rather than negative language. One way to detect negative language is to look for words like can't, don't, and words with negative prefixes. Example: prefer To get a donut, stand in line over You can't get a donut if you don't stand in line.

## Contractions, Conciseness, and Specificity
Contractions are encouraged: they give writing an informal, friendly tone. Use short words and short sentences, avoid unnecessary modifiers, cut vague language, and eliminate fluff.

## Mechanics
Always use the serial (Oxford) comma: David admires his parents, Oprah, and Justin Timberlake. Spell out a number that begins a sentence, otherwise use numerals including ordinals; add commas to numbers over three digits; use the percent symbol for percentages. Spell out an unfamiliar abbreviation on first mention, then use the short form; well known abbreviations like API or HTML need no introduction. Note that Mailchimp keeps the Oxford comma while AP style drops it, a reminder that a house style must choose one convention and hold it.

title: David Ogilvy, Headline and Copy Principles (reproduced)
text:
## The Weight of the Headline
David Ogilvy: on the average, five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. When you have written your headline, you have spent eighty cents out of your dollar. It follows that unless your headline sells your product, you have wasted most of your money.

## Facts Over Puffery
Factual advertising outsells flatulent puffery: the more you tell, the more you sell. Ogilvy's most famous headline used pure specificity: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. A concrete, verifiable fact carries more persuasion than any adjective.

## Named Rules
Every headline should appeal to the reader's self interest and promise a benefit. Single out the prospect: a headline aimed at gin and tonic drinkers should say so, rather than speaking to everyone and no one. Simplify the language: use short words, short sentences, short paragraphs, and avoid vocabulary that confuses, such as obsolete or ineffable. Provide specifics: state a precise figure such as a real weekly price rather than a vague claim of affordability, and back it up. Give the image story appeal so it arouses the reader's curiosity.

## Lesson for Content Writers
Ogilvy's craft is the antidote to vague, self congratulatory content: lead with a concrete benefit, use plain short words, prove claims with specifics, and remember that the headline is where most of the reader's attention (and most of your effort) belongs.

title: Google Technical Writing One, Write Clear Sentences
text:
## Choose Strong Verbs
The verb is the most important part of a sentence. Replace weak, generic verbs (forms of be, occur, happen) with precise, specific ones. Example: This error message happens when... becomes The system generates this error message when...

## Prefer Active Voice
Most sentences should be in active voice, where the actor performs the action on a target, rather than passive voice, which hides or delays the actor. Active voice is usually shorter, clearer, and unambiguous about who does what.

## Reduce There Is and There Are
These phrases pair a generic noun with a generic verb and bury the real subject. Delete them, or move the true subject and verb to the start of the sentence. Example: There are two disturbing facts about Perl you should know becomes You should know two disturbing facts about Perl.

## Minimize Adjectives and Adverbs
Descriptive words tend to be subjective and can read like marketing. Replace them with objective, numerical information. Example: makes the application run screamingly fast becomes makes the application run 225 to 250 percent faster.

## Core Philosophy
Clarity takes precedence over all other rules. Educate the reader with factual data rather than persuasive language. One idea per sentence keeps the reader oriented.

title: Google Technical Writing One, Lists and Tables
text:
## Choose the Right List Type
Use a bulleted list for unordered items where rearranging them does not change the meaning. Use a numbered list for ordered items where sequence matters. Avoid embedded (run-in) lists inside a sentence; convert them to a bulleted or numbered list instead.

## Keep List Items Parallel
All items in a parallel list match along four parameters: grammar, logical category, capitalization, and punctuation. Nonparallel lists read as sloppy and are harder to scan. For a numbered list of steps, start each item with an imperative verb such as open or start, which makes the instructions clear and consistent.

## Punctuation and Capitalization
Start each list item with a capital letter (with some exceptions) and use sentence ending punctuation for items that are complete sentences. Keep the choice consistent across the list.

## Introduce Lists and Tables
Always introduce a list or table with a sentence that sets context, and terminate that introductory sentence with a colon rather than a period. Using the word following in the lead in signals that a list or table is coming.

## Tables
Label columns with meaningful headers, keep items within a column parallel, and avoid putting too much text into a cell: if a cell holds more than two sentences, ask whether that information belongs in another format. Lists and tables are core scannability tools, they turn dense prose into structure a reader can absorb at a glance.
